# structural — do tree/outline searches help structural questions? (`EVAL-2`)

**Template-generated by the author. Not human-judged, not an external benchmark.**
This set exists to answer one question with a number:

> When someone asks "what does chapter 2 say about …" or "summarise section 3.4",
> does letting a retriever navigate a document's section hierarchy put the right
> pages first, compared with the same retriever without it?

The corpus is the two ViDoRe v3 collections `kb-eval` already has: two OpenStax
computer-science textbooks (1,360 pages) and fourteen EU employment reports
(1,110 pages), 16 PDFs and 2,470 pages in total. The queries are built from the
PDFs' own outlines, so the gold page of a section is the page its bookmark
points at — a proxy for relevance, not a person's judgement.

Everything here is deterministic: the same PDFs produce the same
`outlines.json`, and the same outlines produce the same queries and qrels
(seed 42). No model is called, no network is touched, and there is no paid
component anywhere in this set.

## Files

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `outlines.json` | every document's section tree: title, level, start page, end page, extraction method (153 KB) |
| `queries.jsonl` | 80 queries, BEIR `{"_id", "text"}` |
| `query-meta.jsonl` | per query: template, document, outline node, heading title, level, gold pages |
| `qrels/test.tsv` | 297 page judgements, three columns (`qid<TAB><doc>#p<N><TAB>grade`), the format every kb-eval set uses |
| `spot-check.txt` | ten random gold entries checked against `pdftotext` of the page (10/10 passed) |
| `corpus/` | **symlinks** to `../../../datasets/vidore3-{cs,hr}-en/corpus/*.pdf`, so `kb-server eval --dataset` sees one corpus |

`corpus/` holds symlinks because the PDFs are imported, git-ignored data
(`import_vidore.py`), not repository content. If the links are dangling, the
ViDoRe datasets have not been imported in this checkout — see
[Before you run](#before-you-run).

## The outline (`outline.py`)

For each PDF, `outline.py` reads the PDF's bookmark tree through
`pdftohtml -xml -i -stdout` (only page 1 is rendered; the outline is still
emitted, so a 945-page book costs about 0.2 s). A bookmark's `page` is the
**1-based PDF page**, the same numbering as `<doc>#p<N>` in ViDoRe qrels: page
17 of the Python book is `Introduction_to_Python_Programming#p17`, where
"Chapter 1 Statements" starts.

If a PDF has no bookmarks, it falls back to numbered headings found by
`pdftotext -layout` per page ("3.4 Title", "Chapter 3", "2.1.1 Title"),
skipping table-of-contents pages first so a heading is not "found" on the
contents page. The method is recorded per document.

Levels come from the bookmark nesting, except that a title carrying its own
numbering (`2.1.1`) overrides the nesting: Poppler omits bookmark parents that
have no destination, so some reports nest a chapter's children at the wrong
depth while the number in the title is exact. End pages follow "the page before
the next heading at the same or a higher level", with one exception: a
"Chapter N" heading ends at the next "Chapter M" heading, because an outline
whose bookmarks are all flat would otherwise give every chapter a one-page span.

Measured on this host (Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4, 8 vCPU, Poppler 24.02.0), second
run, page cache warm:

```
wall=3.51s  user=2.90s  sys=0.59s  maxrss=29MB
2,470 pages, 16 PDFs, 626 outline nodes
```

That is about **1.4 ms of wall time per page** and **no model call**. A
bookmark-less PDF is the slow case (~4 ms/page for the 202-page report below,
because `pdftotext` reads the whole document); a scanned, image-only PDF yields
no headings and is reported as method `none` rather than guessed at.

| Document | Method | Pages | Nodes |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `Introduction_to_Computer_Science` | bookmarks | 945 | 114 |

## The query set (`generate_structural.py`)

80 queries: 39 from the CS textbooks, 41 from the HR reports. 50 name an
explicit number, 30 give only the heading's words; 19 target a chapter-level
node and 61 a section-level one (50 at level 2, 11 at level 3).

| Template | CS | HR | Example |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `section_topic` — number + topic words | 13 | 13 | "What does the Python book cover in section 2.6 on math module?" |
| `section_number` — number only | 8 | 6 | "Summarise section 2.3.1 of the Joint Employment Report 2025." |
| `section_title` — title words, no number | 8 | 13 | "In the Python book, what is covered in the section titled \"Formatted strings\"?" |
| `chapter_number` | 8 | 2 | "Summarise chapter 5 of Introduction to Computer Science." |
| `chapter_title` — no number | 2 | 7 | "In the Joint Employment Report 2025, what is in the chapter on first-stage country analysis?" |

Three phrasings rotate within each template (e.g. "What does … say about …",
"What does … cover in section …", "Find the part of … that explains …"), and
the document is named by its title or by a natural alias ("the Python book").
The generator picks nodes not already used, samples with seed 42, and refuses
to write a set with a missing quota.

### Gold, and why it stops at five pages

For a target heading, gold is its first five pages: grade **2** for the heading
page and grade **1** for the next four (clamped to the heading's end page).
Chapters run to 30+ pages; marking all of them relevant makes the ideal nDCG@10
unreachable with ten results and makes every system's score a small number that
barely moves. Five pages is the heading plus the opening of the section — what
"what does chapter 2 say" should land on. The trade-off is that recall@10 is
recall over at most five pages, so 0.6 means "three of the five gold pages in
the top ten", not "60% of the chapter".

## Known biases — read these before believing a number

1. **Circular by construction.** The queries are generated from the same
   outlines the tree arm consumes. Offline the arm puts the exact heading page
   first for 79/80 queries and a gold page in its top five for 80/80. That
   proves the plumbing lines up; it is **not**
   evidence that a tree index helps, because no baseline competed with it.
2. **Lexically easy.** Every non-numbered query quotes or paraphrases the
   heading, and the heading is printed at the top of the gold page. A plain
   BM25 baseline can match those words without any hierarchy. A gain on this
   set is therefore an upper bound on what title matching buys, not on what
   hierarchy buys.
3. **The document is always named.** "What does section 4.2 of the Python book
   say about loops?" Every generated query names its document; real users often
   do not. Document selection is therefore handed to the retriever for free.
4. **Gold is the outline, not a judgement.** A bookmark can point at a summary
   page or a chapter opener. ESDE 2024's "Chapter 1/2/3" bookmarks point into
   the executive summary, so chapter nodes whose span is shorter than four
   pages were excluded; the labour-market report has a bookmark out of document
   order ("1.3" listed after an annex), so the whole document is excluded from
   query generation. Both exclusions live in `generate_structural.py`.
5. **Flat outlines make weak "chapters".** The undeclared-care-work report's
   bookmarks carry no nesting; only its three explicit "Chapter N" headings are
   used at chapter level. In reports whose top-level bookmarks are parts of a
   chapter (ESDE 2024), a "chapter on …" query can target a top-level part.
6. **Numbered headings share words.** "Key indicators" and "Measures taken by
   Member States" repeat across the Joint Employment Report. They are kept for
   number-bearing templates (the number disambiguates) and excluded from
   title-only templates (the title does not).
7. **Author's templates, not users' words.** The phrasings are plausible, not
   observed. A real query log would be a better instrument; divergences from
   these templates are exactly what a follow-up human-labelled set should fix.

Ten random gold entries were checked against `pdftotext` (`spot-check.txt`,
seed 42): **10/10 passed** — the heading (or at least 60% of its content words)
is on its grade-2 page. One of the ten, "Chapter 2: Consequences of undeclared
care work", matched on its title words rather than the literal string
"chapter 2" because the page sets the chapter number as a running head; that is
recorded in the file rather than smoothed over.

## The prototype arms

### `tree_arm.py`

Scores outline nodes per query and writes a page-level TREC run
(`qid Q0 <doc>#p<N> rank score tree`):

* explicit numbers: `section 4.2`, `§ 4.2`, `chapter 5`, or a bare `4.2` match
  the heading's number (a chapter number also partially matches its `N.x`
  children, but the chapter node wins);
* BM25 over node titles with the document title folded in (k1 1.2, b 0.75);
* document selection by query-token vote over the document title and file key,
  restricted to the winner only when it wins clearly;
* at most five nodes × five pages, 50 pages total.

No index is built and nothing is stored: it loads `outlines.json` per run.

### `tree_fuse.py`

Reciprocal-rank fusion of a baseline page run (from `kb-server eval`) and the
tree run: `w_base/(k+rank_base) + w_tree/(k+rank_tree)`, `k=60`, configurable
weights (defaults 1.0 and 1.0; a prototype probably wants `--tree-weight 0.5`).

`--gate` fuses only queries that look structural and copies every other
query's baseline rows unchanged, so a gated run cannot hurt an ordinary query
by construction. The cue list is chapter/section/subsection/part/appendix/
annex/contents/§, a dotted number or `<noun> N`, and the report-scaffolding
vocabulary in `rust/crates/kb-core/src/intelligence/heuristic.rs` (the "Report
scaffolding and titles" block). **Note:** `rust/crates/kb-core/src/query_class.rs`
is cited in the brief as the Rust structural classifier, but that file has no
structural branch — it only separates exact/identifier queries from natural
ones. The gate reuses its token normalisation (lower-case, strip surrounding
punctuation) and takes its cue words from `heuristic.rs`; the gate itself is
new code here, not a port.

On the regular ViDoRe query sets the gate fires on **7/215 CS (3.3%)** and
**24/318 HR (7.5%)** queries. Some of those are false positives ("…as mentioned
in the summary"), which is why the ungated run is also part of the runbook: the
gate's precision is a variable, not an assumption.

## Before you run

The PDFs are imported data, not repo content:

```sh
uv run rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/import_vidore.py \
  --dataset vidore/vidore_v3_computer_science --language english \
  --out rust/crates/kb-eval/datasets/vidore3-cs-en
uv run rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/import_vidore.py \
  --dataset vidore/vidore_v3_hr --language english \
  --out rust/crates/kb-eval/datasets/vidore3-hr-en
ls -L rust/crates/kb-eval/sets/structural/corpus | head   # links must resolve
```

Regenerating the set (deterministic; only needed if a PDF or the generator
changes):

```sh
python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/outline.py
python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/generate_structural.py
python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/spot_check_structural.py
```

## Runbook — the live measurement (for the planner)

The scripts below build the instruments. The numbers that decide `DEC-4` come
from running the real service, which needs a stack, an API key and the imported
datasets. `kb-server eval` writes both `run.trec` (document level) and
`run.page.trec` (page level); every comparison here uses the page run, because
the qrels are page-level.

### (a) Baseline runs

One tenant per dataset. `kb-server eval` searches everything the key can see, so
mixing the CS, HR and structural corpora in one tenant would add the other
documents as unjudged distractors.

```sh
export KB_EVAL_API_KEY=<key-for-a-fresh-tenant>
BASE=http://localhost:3000
OUT=docs/eval-ab/eval2

# structural set: 80 queries, 16 PDFs (the union of both ViDoRe corpora)
cargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p kb-server -- eval \
  --base-url "$BASE" --api-key "$KB_EVAL_API_KEY" \
  --dataset rust/crates/kb-eval/sets/structural \
  --out "$OUT/structural/baseline" --label tree-off --max-chunks 100

# regular sets, unchanged queries and qrels
cargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p kb-server -- eval \
  --base-url "$BASE" --api-key "$KB_EVAL_API_KEY" \
  --dataset rust/crates/kb-eval/datasets/vidore3-cs-en \
  --out "$OUT/vidore3-cs-en/baseline" --label tree-off --max-chunks 100
cargo run --release --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p kb-server -- eval \
  --base-url "$BASE" --api-key "$KB_EVAL_API_KEY" \
  --dataset rust/crates/kb-eval/datasets/vidore3-hr-en \
  --out "$OUT/vidore3-hr-en/baseline" --label tree-off --max-chunks 100
```

Re-running the same `--out` with `--skip-ingest` reuses `ingest-map.json`; it
does not re-upload and does not need the ingest budget.

### (b) Tree runs and fusion

The tree run needs no server and no index; it reads `outlines.json` and the
dataset's `queries.jsonl`.

```sh
for SET in structural vidore3-cs-en vidore3-hr-en; do
  if [ "$SET" = structural ]; then Q=rust/crates/kb-eval/sets/structural/queries.jsonl
  else Q=rust/crates/kb-eval/datasets/$SET/queries.jsonl; fi
  python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/tree_arm.py \
    --outlines rust/crates/kb-eval/sets/structural/outlines.json \
    --queries "$Q" --out "$OUT/$SET/tree.trec" --explain 2>"$OUT/$SET/tree.explain.txt"

  # treatment: gated tree arm on top of the same baseline
  python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/tree_fuse.py \
    --baseline "$OUT/$SET/baseline/run.page.trec" --tree "$OUT/$SET/tree.trec" \
    --queries "$Q" --gate --tree-weight 0.5 --out "$OUT/$SET/fused-gated.trec"

  # sensitivity: ungated, to see what the tree arm does to ordinary questions
  python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/tree_fuse.py \
    --baseline "$OUT/$SET/baseline/run.page.trec" --tree "$OUT/$SET/tree.trec" \
    --queries "$Q" --tree-weight 0.5 --out "$OUT/$SET/fused-ungated.trec"
done
```

### (c) Score, tree on vs off

```sh
for SET in structural vidore3-cs-en vidore3-hr-en; do
  if [ "$SET" = structural ]; then QRELS=rust/crates/kb-eval/sets/structural/qrels/test.tsv
  else QRELS=rust/crates/kb-eval/datasets/$SET/qrels/test.tsv; fi
  for TREATMENT in fused-gated fused-ungated; do
    echo "=== $SET: $TREATMENT"
    python3 rust/crates/kb-eval/scripts/score_deltas.py \
      --qrels "$QRELS" \
      --baseline "$OUT/$SET/baseline/run.page.trec" \
      --treatment "$OUT/$SET/$TREATMENT.trec"
  done
done
```

`score_deltas.py` reports recall@5, recall@10, MRR@10 and nDCG@10 with paired
per-query deltas and a 95% percentile bootstrap interval (10,000 resamples,
seed 42). The decision rule for `DEC-4` is already written there: keep the tree
plane only if its structural-set gain has a 95% CI above zero **and** the
regular ViDoRe sets do not lose. Both gated and ungated runs are scored because
the gate's precision is part of what has to be measured.

For a second, independent read of the same page run, `kb-server eval score`
computes nDCG from a run file with no server; it is a cross-check, not the
paired comparison.

## Offline plumbing checks (not results)

Run on 2026-11-04 with a synthetic oracle baseline built from this set's qrels
and an empty run, to prove `tree_arm.py` → `tree_fuse.py` → `score_deltas.py`
work end to end. **These numbers say nothing about retrieval quality.**

| Check | What it proves | Result |
|---|---|---|
| oracle baseline fused with an **empty** tree run | RRF with one list is order-preserving | 80 queries, all deltas `+0.0000 [+0.0000, +0.0000]` |
| **empty** baseline vs tree run alone | the arm emits the gold pages it derived | recall@10 1.0000, nDCG@10 0.9988 (not 1.0: dedupe can put a grade-1 page before a grade-2 one) |
| oracle baseline fused with the tree run, `--tree-weight 0.5` | gold pages survive fusion | all deltas `+0.0000`, 80/80 |
| gated fusion on regular ViDoRe + oracle baseline | the gate leaves ordinary queries byte-identical | 208/215 CS and 294/318 HR queries copied unchanged; nDCG@10 -0.0005 / -0.0014, only on the gated subset |

## What this set cannot tell you

* whether a **real** baseline gets better with the tree arm — that needs the
  live runs in the runbook;
* whether the outline is the right granularity for a user ("chapter 2" spans
  30 pages in a textbook);
* whether headings in an image-only PDF can be recovered — the fallback is
  text-only, and those documents are marked `none`;
* anything about tenants, scoping or cost beyond the measured CPU above.
